text:
想入门 AI 领域的极佳方式就是大量的翻阅论文，我身边朋友的例子就是韭二老师 （@li9292）。通过爆肝60篇 AI 论文，直接入职盛大集团投资产品 evermind

并且学习论文还可以一并在 x 中直接分发，也是种暴力起号的方式，这个赛道绝对是一片空白，你去翻翻英文区的论文流量，就知道有多夸张

但如果你还是担心自己是个论文小白，我强烈推荐使用 Open-Science快速入门，其是一个一体化AI 科研工作台。无论你是学生，或者是任何对研究感兴趣的人， 都可以通过Open-Science进行科研project复现，比如复现前沿科学或者前沿科学家的项目。只要复现5篇以上，包成为 AI 领域的专家

用它自己的愿景来说：Open-Science希望降低科研工具的使用门槛，让每一个有好奇心、有研究想法的人，都能更容易地参与研究，并通过开放共享的工具和方法，连接全球科研者

而从我自己的体验，其具体有几个亮点比较吸引我：

1、平台上的Agent专为论文研究设计，并内置科研skills，你只需要清晰描述你的目标任务，它就能从学术数据库中检索相关文献、梳理研究方法，并交付最终的报告

2、模型选择灵活。支持接入不同的模型，也能直接使用已有的 Codex、Claude 订阅，我们可以根据具体任务来合适分配

3、过程和结果方便回溯查看。所有研究过程中生成的图表、报告均可查看相关输入、代码和执行记录，出问题便于人工审核；项目和运行历史也会保存下来，方便检查和继续研究

4、支持动手实践，验证研究方法：你可以在它的辅助下亲自复现论文中的计算与分析，从而深入理解研究过程及结论

Open-Science开源仓库链接：https://t.co/0L7Do2Tv6q

A 3B active model beats Opus 5 at memory. We open-sourced the full stack — model, engine, and app.

Hy Memory handles chat, work, and code memory in one layer, and it's first on all four benchmarks we ran, leading MemoryArena by 10.2 points while cutting memory volume 51.8% and recall tokens 39.3%.

The model isn't tied to our engine. Drop Hy-Memory-30B-A3B into Mem0, MemOS, or EverMemOS and it still comes out on top, even on the one system it never trained on. It's already running in our own products, where one assistant's multi-hop recall went from 50% to 90%. It also unifies memory across Codex, Cursor, WorkBuddy, and more.

text:
卧槽！TradingView 上专抓假突破的量化策略，居然有人把源码直接开源了！

价格刚突破就掉头？连这种行情的反向交易逻辑，都有人写成了 Pine Script。

这个开源项目叫 TradingView_Indicators。

作者 Heavy91 开源了 3 个技术指标和 1 套交易策略，涵盖假突破、多周期 RSI、成交量供需区和均线交叉信号。

几个挺硬核的能力：

1️⃣ Failure Swing：专门研究假突破，价格突破关键位置后又收回，寻找反向交易机会。

2️⃣ 动态止盈止损：结合 EMA 和波动率，设计交易退出条件。

3️⃣ 多周期 RSI：同时观察周线、日线和 4 小时 RSI，识别超买超卖共振。

4️⃣ 成交量供需区：通过 3 档成交量阈值识别关键区域，支持跨周期显示。

5️⃣ 多周期均线：支持 EMA、SMA、WMA、VWMA 等均线，监控趋势和交叉信号。

我比较感兴趣的是 Failure Swing。

很多人做量化只研究突破成功后的行情，而它专门研究突破失败后，如何利用价格重新回到区间的机会。

再结合多周期 RSI 和成交量供需区，就能进一步研究一套有明确进出场规则的量化策略。

最关键的是，指标和策略源码都能直接拆解、修改，不用从零开发。

经常使用 TradingView、研究价格行为，或者开发股票量化策略的，这套源码值得收藏。

https://t.co/7PtYKFFQB7

quotedTweet.text:
绝了！LuxAlgo 居然把交易复盘终端直接开源了！

券商同步、盈亏分析、K 线回放，甚至 AI 自动复盘交易习惯，都给安排好了。

项目叫 Trade Journal，GitHub 474 Stars、182 Forks，MIT 协议。

它是一套免费、支持本地部署的交易分析系统，不只是记录盈亏，还能帮你研究策略表现、交易失误和风险。

几个挺硬核的能力：

1️⃣ 多券商同步：支持 IBKR、Alpaca、Webull、Binance 等，还能导入 TradingView、MT4/MT5 交易记录。

2️⃣ 深度绩效分析：自动计算胜率、盈亏比、最大回撤，按品种、时间和交易习惯拆解表现。

3️⃣ 盈亏日历：直观展示每日收益、连续亏损和交易统计，还有公开计算公式的 Edge Score。

4️⃣ K 线交易回放：标记进出场位置，回放历史行情，分析交易过程中错过的机会。

5️⃣ AI 智能复盘：接入 OpenAI、Claude，让 AI 总结交易、分析失误，还能直接提问自己的交易记录。

6️⃣ MCP + AI Agent：LuxAlgo 托管版提供 13 个交易日志 MCP 工具，可接入 Claude、ChatGPT 等客户端。

我觉得它最有意思的，是让交易复盘不再只是看收益曲线。

比如让 AI 分析过去 90 天的交易，找出哪些时间段最容易亏损、哪些策略表现不稳定，再结合历史交易记录研究原因。

原本需要自己整理的数据，现在可以集中到一套系统里分析。

而且支持本地 SQLite 存储，不需要把完整交易日志上传到第三方平台。

它不是自动交易机器人，而是一套帮助交易者发现问题、改进策略的复盘工具。

做股票量化、策略研究或者自动交易的，这个项目值得收藏。

https://t.co/jghRYj1gnm

价格刚突破就掉头？连这种行情的反向交易逻辑，都有人写成了 Pine Script。

这个开源项目叫 TradingView_Indicators。

作者 Heavy91 开源了 3 个技术指标和 1 套交易策略，涵盖假突破、多周期 RSI、成交量供需区和均线交叉信号。

几个挺硬核的能力：

1️⃣ Failure Swing：专门研究假突破，价格突破关键位置后又收回，寻找反向交易机会。

2️⃣ 动态止盈止损：结合 EMA 和波动率，设计交易退出条件。

3️⃣ 多周期 RSI：同时观察周线、日线和 4 小时 RSI，识别超买超卖共振。

4️⃣ 成交量供需区：通过 3 档成交量阈值识别关键区域，支持跨周期显示。

5️⃣ 多周期均线：支持 EMA、SMA、WMA、VWMA 等均线，监控趋势和交叉信号。

我比较感兴趣的是 Failure Swing。

很多人做量化只研究突破成功后的行情，而它专门研究突破失败后，如何利用价格重新回到区间的机会。

再结合多周期 RSI 和成交量供需区，就能进一步研究一套有明确进出场规则的量化策略。

最关键的是，指标和策略源码都能直接拆解、修改，不用从零开发。

经常使用 TradingView、研究价格行为，或者开发股票量化策略的，这套源码值得收藏。

https://t.co/7PtYKFFQB7

result.text:
绝了！LuxAlgo 居然把交易复盘终端直接开源了！

券商同步、盈亏分析、K 线回放，甚至 AI 自动复盘交易习惯，都给安排好了。

项目叫 Trade Journal，GitHub 474 Stars、182 Forks，MIT 协议。

它是一套免费、支持本地部署的交易分析系统，不只是记录盈亏，还能帮你研究策略表现、交易失误和风险。

几个挺硬核的能力：

1️⃣ 多券商同步：支持 IBKR、Alpaca、Webull、Binance 等，还能导入 TradingView、MT4/MT5 交易记录。

2️⃣ 深度绩效分析：自动计算胜率、盈亏比、最大回撤，按品种、时间和交易习惯拆解表现。

3️⃣ 盈亏日历：直观展示每日收益、连续亏损和交易统计，还有公开计算公式的 Edge Score。

4️⃣ K 线交易回放：标记进出场位置，回放历史行情，分析交易过程中错过的机会。

5️⃣ AI 智能复盘：接入 OpenAI、Claude，让 AI 总结交易、分析失误，还能直接提问自己的交易记录。

6️⃣ MCP + AI Agent：LuxAlgo 托管版提供 13 个交易日志 MCP 工具，可接入 Claude、ChatGPT 等客户端。

我觉得它最有意思的，是让交易复盘不再只是看收益曲线。

比如让 AI 分析过去 90 天的交易，找出哪些时间段最容易亏损、哪些策略表现不稳定，再结合历史交易记录研究原因。

原本需要自己整理的数据，现在可以集中到一套系统里分析。

而且支持本地 SQLite 存储，不需要把完整交易日志上传到第三方平台。

它不是自动交易机器人，而是一套帮助交易者发现问题、改进策略的复盘工具。

做股票量化、策略研究或者自动交易的，这个项目值得收藏。

https://t.co/jghRYj1gnm

text:
我全职交易将近 3 年了，目前可以以交易为生，虽然跟 X 上赚几十万，几百万的没法比，但也确实是从小资金做起来的。

刚开始做的时候，我也是一直亏，一直亏，看了很多书，学了很多方法，也看了很多老师的课，但我发现其实都没有什么用，大多数人所谓的交易方法，要么就是很复杂，讲得云里雾里的，要么是生搬硬套一些已经存在理论，这个过程确实浪费了我很多时间，如果当时能早点有人跟我说这些，我最起码可以完整参与到牛市的前半段，所以如果你能看到这段话，应该最起码没有浪费你这十秒。目前市场所有的交易系统，交易方法，形态，指标等等，用的全都是100 多年前华尔街的那套东西，有些人只是为了营销卖课卖会员，故意换个名字，新瓶装旧酒，所以在全职交易的这条路上，我学到最重要的一课，就是祛魅。在市场里面交易，每个人都是在裸奔，大庄吃小庄，小庄吃散户，机构里拿 3 万月薪的分析师和 x 上拿 30u 广告的 KOL 并没有什么区别，十万粉的 Kol 和刚入圈的新手也没有什么区别，你一旦对这个市场里的某些机构或者某些人有滤镜，就会很痛苦，陷入深深的自我怀疑，绝对会影响你的判断，哪怕你的判断是对的，也会因为某种滤镜导致最后的结果走错

真正开始盈利的时候，是我已经把该踩的坑踩的差不多了，然后又正好赶上了牛市。如果我刚开始做交易，赚到了钱，我肯定会很开心，肯定自己的能力，认为自己有天赋，但是实际上能在市场里赚钱的原因 60% 都是因为行情和运气，30% 来自仓位和心态，这部分说到底还是能不能拿得住，剩下的 10% 才来自你的交易系统。但是为什么明明 10% 才来自交易系统，因为只有这 10% 才是属于你真正能掌握的东西，行情可遇不可求，仓位大小根据每个人的经济水平而决定，至于心态，比较玄学，只能自己悟。所以很多人喜欢去聊技术分析，模式和系统，争执不休，其实你可以只看形态，可以只看指标，可以只看均线，上方做多，下方做空，可以只用裸 K，当你和一些能赚钱的交易员交流你会发现，每个人赚钱的方法都不一样，你要是挨个去学，没个三年五年根本学不过来，但是每个人亏钱的原因都是那么几种，其中我觉得最容易亏钱的一种原因就是什么钱都想赚，既想赚横盘震荡的钱，又想赚上涨的钱，还想赚下跌的钱，盈亏同源，什么钱都想赚，也就意味着会把所有可能踩的坑全踩一遍，这就是因果。

关于交易的技巧和心得太多了，以后有时间慢慢讲吧

quotedTweet.text:
非常精辟

但是我觉得日内交易的精力消耗没有趋势交易大，我觉得任何一个新手都应该从日内交易开始，因为对一个没有足够市场经验的人来说，你去做趋势交易，一旦刚开始的方向选错，那么一整段行情就错过了

日内交易确实消耗精力，不过可以有个方式解决，就是降低仓位，设置固定止盈止损，只验证系统，赚了就走，亏了就割

只要保持正 ev，肯定是能赚钱的

真正开始盈利的时候，是我已经把该踩的坑踩的差不多了，然后又正好赶上了牛市。如果我刚开始做交易，赚到了钱，我肯定会很开心，肯定自己的能力，认为自己有天赋，但是实际上能在市场里赚钱的原因 60% 都是因为行情和运气，30% 来自仓位和心态，这部分说到底还是能不能拿得住，剩下的 10% 才来自你的交易系统。但是为什么明明 10% 才来自交易系统，因为只有这 10% 才是属于你真正能掌握的东西，行情可遇不可求，仓位大小根据每个人的经济水平而决定，至于心态，比较玄学，只能自己悟。所以很多人喜欢去聊技术分析，模式和系统，争执不休，其实你可以只看形态，可以只看指标，可以只看均线，上方做多，下方做空，可以只用裸 K，当你和一些能赚钱的交易员交流你会发现，每个人赚钱的方法都不一样，你要是挨个去学，没个三年五年根本学不过来，但是每个人亏钱的原因都是那么几种，其中我觉得最容易亏钱的一种原因就是什么钱都想赚，既想赚横盘震荡的钱，又想赚上涨的钱，还想赚下跌的钱，盈亏同源，什么钱都想赚，也就意味着会把所有可能踩的坑全踩一遍，这就是因果。

关于交易的技巧和心得太多了，以后有时间慢慢讲吧

text:
十年前 Elon Musk 对未来的预言，拿到今天对照看

2016 年，当时的 YC 总裁 Sam Altman 在 Y Combinator 采访 Elon Musk。那时 OpenAI 才成立六个月，两人还在一起做这件事，Musk 每周去 OpenAI 待半天。他在访谈里讲了自己对 AI、火星、基因和脑机接口的判断。十年过去，可以逐条对一对了。

十年后对照

10:13 「让相当数量的人去火星，大约十年能实现，也许九年。」
今天，还没有人去。今年 2 月 SpaceX 推迟了原定今年的无人火星任务，先去月球，目标 2027 年 3 月无人登月。官网写的是火星货运最早 2028 年。

11:49 「AI 技术要民主化，没有哪一家公司或一小撮人掌控先进 AI。」12:55 他说这正是他和 Sam 创办 OpenAI 的原因。
今天，Musk 2018 年离开 OpenAI 董事会，2023 年自己创办 xAI。OpenAI 去年 10 月完成重组，营利部分变成公益公司，非营利基金会仍然控股。Musk 起诉 OpenAI 和 Altman，今年 5 月陪审团认定他起诉超过时效，诉讼被驳回，他表示会上诉。今年接受 The Economist 采访时，他直说「我不喜欢 Sam Altman」。

1:51 「如果能用基因重编程解决遗传病，那就太好了。」他把遗传学排在 AI 之后，第二重要。
今天，2023 年 12 月，美国 FDA 批准了第一款 CRISPR 基因编辑疗法 Casgevy，用来治镰状细胞病。

2:16 「我们和数字化的自己之间，带宽极其受限。」14:07 他说最好的结果是人通过高带宽接口和 AI 融合。
今天，他创办的 Neuralink 2024 年 1 月完成首例人体植入，第一位患者能用意念控制鼠标。到今年 6 月，全球已有 26 人植入。

视频里还聊了
5:11 怎么判断自己在哪最有用，算效用提升乘以影响人数
5:50 明知很疯狂，还是做了 SpaceX，自己估的胜算不到 10%
8:16 他其实很怕，只是怕也照样去做
18:04 今年最大的顿悟，造车的工厂比车本身难两个数量级

金句摘录
4:49 「我真的只是想做点有用的事。这就是我优化的目标。」
7:55 「熵不站在你这边。」
8:46 「感到恐惧是正常的。不害怕才说明你心理有问题。」

配了中英双语字幕，原视频链接在回复里。

4️⃣ Automated cron/bots → Calling consumer plans via scripts
5️⃣ Security prompts → Running cyber/red-team code without enterprise clearance

Export your local `.md` context regularly once this screen hits, there is no second appeal.

而现在的 Argon 的文笔则舒服太多，自然干净、节奏流畅，娓娓道来。

text:
Everyone is talking about how profound this essay is rn. 

For the non-technical person (like myself), a 65-minute read about the inner-workings of neural networks feels very unapproachable. 

But people are right, this essay is profound. And it's important to understand its essence even if you don't grok the particulars. 

So let me do my best to break it down as I understand it...

Let's start with mechanistic interpretability. 

That's what this essay is about & what the field has been obsessed with for a long time. 

Mechanistic interpretability is a clunky phrase, but all it means is the process of understanding how an AI model works on the inside: 
1) which parts of the model do what
2) how they work together to produce an answer

The next obvious question is: why do we even care about understanding how an AI model's internals work? 

There are several reasons, and they all boil down to one word: trust. 

reason 1: we've been building ai we don't understand. unlike every other high-stakes technology (computers, internet, planes, medicine), we know if a model works, but we don't know how it works. 

reason 2: predicting performance is unpredictable. the way ai is judged today is through tests. problem is, tests don't cover enough ground. a model can perform well in testing, but not deployment. you can't run every test possible. and a model can give you the right answer for the wrong reason. 

reason 3: scanning for deception is important. as models get better, there's concern that models will output one thing, while "thinking" something else. if you can only understand outputs, a model can hide its true intentions from you. 

reason 4: it allows for precision when improving the model. once you know which internal parts cause what outputs, you can isolate fixes without having to retrain the entire model and praying it works. 

reason 5: understanding how the model works is mission critical in high-risk industries. simply saying the model did the right thing "just because" to stakeholders in healthcare, financial services, and government won't fly especially as regulation matures around this technology. 

reason 6: humans can learn from how the models "think". models sometimes learn patterns that humans haven't. if we understand their thought processes we can leverage those for humanity's own novel insights. 

So, that's why mechanistic interpretability is important. 

Next, it's important to understand why there's been so much focus & concern around this area of AI research for a while now. 

Prior to this piece by @nickcammarata, the consensus view was...

Progress has been made in the field over the years (from studying toy models to massive production models in short order), but even still, current techniques are slow, expensive, and only cover small parts of understanding a model. 

And here's the rough story researchers have generally agreed on re: why the practice of interpretability has remained limited: 

1) AI models are built from millions of “neurons,” small units that each light up in response to a given input. 

2) Ideally every neuron has one clear job, that way you can map out the model as a diagram of neurons and their corresponding meaning cleanly. Example: there's a "dog ear detector" neuron and it fires on floppy dog ears, from any breed, angle, or photo, and on nothing else. 

3) There's a problem: early researchers found that neurons had several unrelated jobs (i.e. they fired on unrelated inputs). The most famous example was of a neuron that fired on both cat faces and fronts of cars. 

4) The leading explanation for "messy" neurons was called superposition. The idea was that when a model runs out of room (i.e. more concepts it wants to track than it has neurons to track them with), it crams unrelated concepts into the same neuron because they rarely show up together. 

5) If this theory of superposition is true, studying neurons would be a fools errand, because you'd have to use a second AI model (called a sparse autoencoder) to try and untangle the first model, which would be expensive & potentially offer an incorrect understanding of the original model. 

Which left mechanistic interpretability in this weird spot. As @nickcammarata points out, it is arguably the most important scientific problem to solve as it helps us understand the most powerful technology in human history, but vibes around cracking the code have been lackluster. 

In his new essay, Nick, who has pioneered much of the recent work being done in interpretability, posits that the field has largely thought about this problem incorrectly & he explains why. 

Which, if he's right, is hugely positive for the world. 

Here's his argument...

He believes that neural networks are in fact largely readable, and the "tangled mess" narrative is oversold as a fundamental property, when it's really solvable problems. 

He breaks this belief down into four steps: 

"1) Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them."

Translation: Neural networks group things by shared patterns (generalization). They don’t switch to cramming unrelated things together when space runs out (superposition) as mentioned above.

"2) With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect."

Translation: you can study neural nets just as you study anything with science. Assume the neurons are mostly readable as they are. Study the real model directly. And test your explanations with experiments.

"3) Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit."

Translation: studying models gets easier as technology and tooling gets better + as you start filling in your understanding of the model it becomes easier to complete the rest. Think of it like a crossword. Each neuron you explain becomes a reference point for checking the ones around it. Early on, a guess about a neuron has nothing to be checked against. Later, it has to fit with everything connected to it, so wrong guesses get caught and right ones get confirmed quickly

"4) Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed."

Translation: if steps 1-3 hold and scale, direct investigation might take us most of the way to understand an AI model & possibly soon. The reasoning is that models have finite number of neurons, most are readable and AI agents can audit them at scale, understanding compounds (crossword effect), so mapping a model is a large, but finite engineering problem. 

He goes on to share evidence for his changing worldview as well as steelman the weaker parts of his argument. 

First, evidence. Cammarata provides 8 supporting cases. 

1) The case for superposition relied heavily on two examples from vision models and they were misread
- The cat/car neuron turned out to detect pointed V shapes. It was also activated when detecting flames, fox snouts, and other pointy things and went negative when round shapes were presented. 
- The car-detecting neuron that appeared to be "stashed" inside dog neurons were found to not be dog neurons but instead pose neurons: which detected the orientation of an object. Cars and dogs can both be in a head-on pose which would activate the neuron. 

2) InceptionV1 an image-recognition model from 2014 was the first model researchers studied closely. It's early layers were easy to read (neurons for edges, curves, colors), but it's final layer (where the model makes abstract judgements), looked like nonsense. Almost no neurons could be described (0-5%) understandable. This became industry evidence for the "Neural nets are hopelessly tangled" view. 

Nick argues that this model had very explainable problems (a bad camera & a poorly built model), and everyone through the baby out with the bath water. 

3) Superposition theory says that when a model runs out of neurons, it starts cramming unrelated things together. So Nick deliberately took neurons away (480 --> 10) to see if that happens. It did not, the model just started using broader categories. Think of it as a finance org going from five finance specialists to one person handling all of finance. 

4) Recursive generalization explains the leftover mess. The leftover mess is that some neurons still look messy even in good models. But as Cammarata watched neurons form during model training, he found that this "mess" builds up through a chain of small, coherent jumps the neurons make as the model is trained. Think of a tree. A trunk splits into branches, which split into smaller branches, which split again. If you only saw three leaves from far-apart twigs, they might seem unrelated. Follow the branches back and they all connect to the same trunk.

5) If neurons were scrambled (via superpositioning), an untangling tool (sparse autoencoder mentioned earlier), should have uncovered many hidden concepts the neurons don't show. Instead, about 88% of what it found was just copies of existing neurons. Meaning the model had already organized itself into clean units, so the untangling step just rediscovered what was there. 

6) Superposition believers think that rare concepts might be secretly stashed in hidden combinations of neurons where no one would notice them. Cammarata test this theory by checking all the hiding spots. He found that the model doesn't have a hidden layer of secret machinery. Even when it handles, rare, weird or random things it uses the same known neurons it uses for everything else. 

7) People worry that image models may be clean to interpret but not language models. This comes from two efforts in 2023 to read language neurons where Anthropic found the average neuron to be a 0 (on a 0-14 scale of how understandable it was) and OpenAI found only 1.7% of neurons understandable. But after Nick's audits of 1,000 neurons within Qwen3-32B, he found 90% have one main job, 7% have two related jobs, and 2-4% are random mixtures. Several changes caused greater neuron understandability: bigger, better models, much better AI research assistants, grading for correctness, knowing what to look for, better data to test on, and the crossword effect. 

8) His response to "If neurons are this readable, why did so many smart researchers including himself, believe the opposite for years?" An analogy for his explanation is roughly doctors studying x-rays with a blurry, miscalibrated machine, the only have small low-quality scans, they've never been taught what certain healthy structures look like, and there's a popular theory that the organ is naturally deformed. 

Finally, the weaker parts of his argument he calls out. 

1) Language model evidence is thin. Most of the detailed, controlled experiments are on image models. For language models, he has audits and case studies, and the detailed technical paper isn’t out yet.

2) There's subjectivity in the headline numbers around understanding the job of each neuron. “90% have one job” depends on what counts as one job, how far into the faint signals you look, and how related two things must be to count as the same.

3) Faint signals don’t have a trusted test yet. That’s exactly where superposition defenders would now say the hidden concepts are.

Recap: AI models may be much less of a black box than we thought. For years, researchers focused on mechanistic interpretability believed the inner workings of neural networks were fundamentally scrambled, so trying to study them directly was hopeless. This essay argues that belief was a mistake caused by weak tools and older AI designs.

quotedTweet.text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

https://t.co/zHij5zwKGT

The reasoning is that models have finite number of neurons, most are readable and AI agents can audit them at scale, understanding compounds (crossword effect), so mapping a model is a large, but finite engineering problem. 

He goes on to share evidence for his changing worldview as well as steelman the weaker parts of his argument. 

First, evidence. Cammarata provides 8 supporting cases. 

1) The case for superposition relied heavily on two examples from vision models and they were misread
- The cat/car neuron turned out to detect pointed V shapes. It was also activated when detecting flames, fox snouts, and other pointy things and went negative when round shapes were presented. 
- The car-detecting neuron that appeared to be "stashed" inside dog neurons were found to not be dog neurons but instead pose neurons: which detected the orientation of an object. Cars and dogs can both be in a head-on pose which would activate the neuron. 

2) InceptionV1 an image-recognition model from 2014 was the first model researchers studied closely. It's early layers were easy to read (neurons for edges, curves, colors), but it's final layer (where the model makes abstract judgements), looked like nonsense. Almost no neurons could be described (0-5%) understandable. This became industry evidence for the "Neural nets are hopelessly tangled" view. 

Nick argues that this model had very explainable problems (a bad camera & a poorly built model), and everyone through the baby out with the bath water. 

3) Superposition theory says that when a model runs out of neurons, it starts cramming unrelated things together. So Nick deliberately took neurons away (480 --> 10) to see if that happens. It did not, the model just started using broader categories. Think of it as a finance org going from five finance specialists to one person handling all of finance. 

4) Recursive generalization explains the leftover mess. The leftover mess is that some neurons still look messy even in good models. But as Cammarata watched neurons form during model training, he found that this "mess" builds up through a chain of small, coherent jumps the neurons make as the model is trained. Think of a tree. A trunk splits into branches, which split into smaller branches, which split again. If you only saw three leaves from far-apart twigs, they might seem unrelated. Follow the branches back and they all connect to the same trunk.

5) If neurons were scrambled (via superpositioning), an untangling tool (sparse autoencoder mentioned earlier), should have uncovered many hidden concepts the neurons don't show. Instead, about 88% of what it found was just copies of existing neurons. Meaning the model had already organized itself into clean units, so the untangling step just rediscovered what was there. 

6) Superposition believers think that rare concepts might be secretly stashed in hidden combinations of neurons where no one would notice them. Cammarata test this theory by checking all the hiding spots. He found that the model doesn't have a hidden layer of secret machinery. Even when it handles, rare, weird or random things it uses the same known neurons it uses for everything else. 

7) People worry that image models may be clean to interpret but not language models. This comes from two efforts in 2023 to read language neurons where Anthropic found the average neuron to be a 0 (on a 0-14 scale of how understandable it was) and OpenAI found only 1.7% of neurons understandable. But after Nick's audits of 1,000 neurons within Qwen3-32B, he found 90% have one main job, 7% have two related jobs, and 2-4% are random mixtures. Several changes caused greater neuron understandability: bigger, better models, much better AI research assistants, grading for correctness, knowing what to look for, better data to test on, and the crossword effect. 

8) His response to "If neurons are this readable, why did so many smart researchers including himself, believe the opposite for years?" An analogy for his explanation is roughly doctors studying x-rays with a blurry, miscalibrated machine, the only have small low-quality scans, they've never been taught what certain healthy structures look like, and there's a popular theory that the organ is naturally deformed. 

Finally, the weaker parts of his argument he calls out. 

1) Language model evidence is thin. Most of the detailed, controlled experiments are on image models. For language models, he has audits and case studies, and the detailed technical paper isn’t out yet.

2) There's subjectivity in the headline numbers around understanding the job of each neuron. “90% have one job” depends on what counts as one job, how far into the faint signals you look, and how related two things must be to count as the same.

3) Faint signals don’t have a trusted test yet. That’s exactly where superposition defenders would now say the hidden concepts are.

Recap: AI models may be much less of a black box than we thought. For years, researchers focused on mechanistic interpretability believed the inner workings of neural networks were fundamentally scrambled, so trying to study them directly was hopeless. This essay argues that belief was a mistake caused by weak tools and older AI designs.

result.text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
If you learn Forward Deployed Engineering, you will never be unemployed again.

I’d do this.

Stage 1: Enterprise Identity & Access (The Gatekeeper)
- Learn:  OAuth2, SAML, OIDC, SCIM provisioning, Row-Level Security (RLS) and multi-tenant data isolation.

- Practice:  Build an auth bridge connecting your AI app to a simulated customer's Okta/Azure AD, ensuring User A can only query data their specific RBAC role permits.

- Why:  No SSO and strict data isolation means no enterprise contract. Security review is the first gate.

Stage 2: Air-Gapped & VPC Deployments (The Environment)
- Learn:  Kubernetes (K8s), Helm, Terraform, private container registries, air-gapped networking and egress filtering.

- Practice:  Script a one-click Terraform/Helm deployment of your entire AI stack into a simulated customer VPC with zero egress to the public internet.

- Why:  Banks, hospitals and governments don't let your AI talk to the public cloud. You must deploy in their basement.

Stage 3: Legacy Data Extraction & ETL (The Fuel)
- Learn:  OCR, unstructured PDF parsing, mainframe DB connectors, Apache Airflow, dbt and data reconciliation.

- Practice:  Build a pipeline that ingests 10 years of messy, scanned customer invoices and turns them into a clean, queryable hybrid (vector + relational) store.

- Why:  Enterprise AI starves without clean data. The customer's data will always be a mess.

Stage 4: Secure RAG & Permission-Filtered Retrieval (The Brain)
- Learn:  Hybrid search, document-level access control, citation grounding, metadata tagging and abstention logic.

- Practice:  Build a RAG pipeline where the LLM dynamically filters out retrieved chunks that the specific user asking the question doesn't have clearance to see.

- Why:  An AI that leaks HR salaries or M&A docs to a junior employee is an immediate breach of contract.

Stage 5: MCP & Legacy System Integration (The Hands)
- Learn:  Model Context Protocol (MCP), SOAP/REST translation, web scraping, headless browsers and API rate-limit handling.

- Practice:  Build an MCP server that lets an LLM safely query and write to the customer's 15-year-old on-prem SAP or Oracle instance without exposing raw credentials.

- Why:  Agents are useless if they can't touch the customer's actual systems of record.

Stage 6: AI Guardrails & PII Redaction (The Shield)
- Learn:  NER (Named Entity Recognition), deterministic regex filtering, LLM output validation, UUID masking, and audit logging.

- Practice:  Build a middleware proxy that intercepts LLM inputs/outputs, masks SSNs and credit cards with UUIDs before they hit the model, and restores them post-generation.

- Why:  Compliance teams will kill the deal if a single PII token hits an external frontier API.

Stage 7: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Workflows (The Trust)
- Learn:  Temporal {dot} io, webhook routing, state machines, durable execution and UI approval gates.

- Practice:  Build a workflow where the AI drafts a $50k purchase order, but physically pauses execution until a human manager clicks "Approve" in Slack or Teams.

- Why:  Enterprises adopt AI only when humans remain legally accountable for the final action.

Stage 8: Edge & On-Prem Inference (The Silicon)
- Learn:  vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Ollama, GPU partitioning (MIG), and local quantized models (AWQ/GGUF).

- Practice:  Deploy a quantized 8B model on a single customer-owned GPU node to handle highly sensitive triage locally without network latency.

- Why:  Sometimes the data is too hot to move. You must bring the model to the data.

Stage 9: Observability & Customer Health (The Pulse)
- Learn:  OpenTelemetry, Langfuse, custom Grafana dashboards, usage telemetry and cost-attribution.

- Practice:  Build a "Customer Health" dashboard showing the exact cost-savings, time-saved and token-spend the AI has generated for their specific team this month.

- Why:  If the customer doesn't see the ROI quantified, they will churn at renewal.

Stage 10: Evals on Customer Data (The Proof)
- Learn:  Golden dataset creation, trajectory grading, shadow testing, and LLM-as-a-judge calibration.

- Practice:  Take 100 real past customer support tickets, run them through your agent in shadow mode, and prove to the VP of Support that it resolved 80% accurately.

- Why:  Generic benchmarks mean nothing to a buyer. You must prove the AI works on *their* messy data.

Stage 11: Technical Discovery & Scoping (The Translation)
- Learn:  Stakeholder interviewing, architecture diagramming, SOW (Statement of Work) writing and expectation management.

- Practice:  Translate a vague "we want AI for supply chain" executive request into a scoped, 4-week technical deployment plan with defined, measurable success metrics.

- Why:  FDEs are the translators between revenue (Sales) and reality (Engineering).

Stage 12: The Handoff & Self-Serve Admin (The Scale)
- Learn:  Technical writing, runbooks, admin portals, automated onboarding and chaos testing.

- Practice:  Write a deployment runbook and build an admin UI so the customer's internal IT team can manage the AI stack, update prompts and view logs without calling you.

- Why:  Your leverage is measured by how little the customer needs you for day-to-day operations.

AI labs build the engine. FDEs build the roads.
The modern Forward Deployed Engineer builds the secure, durable nervous system that connects frontier intelligence to legacy reality.

Bookmark and Repost!

看来我留学的最大意义就是拥有了外国卡和手机号 😂

最近折腾 AI 量化的，可以试试这套提示词
直接交给 Codex 或 Claude Code，让它围绕一个动量思路生成 27 套参数组合，跑回测、算手续费和滑点，再用没参与调参的数据继续筛。
我觉得实用的地方是，它要求把亏钱的策略也列出来，讲清楚哪里容易失效，省得自己盯着一条漂亮曲线越看越上头。
图里的数字是教学示例，具体效果要接自己的数据跑。手里攒了一堆策略、一直没认真验证的，正好拿来整理一轮。

quotedTweet.text:
很多策略亏钱，是行情已经变了，还在用上一套打法。

我在使用的 AI + HMM 的交易系统思路，先判断市场更像趋势、震荡还是高压状态，再决定用哪套策略：有趋势就跟，震荡就做回归，看不清就少做。

AI 负责研究和复盘，仓位、止损、停机这些交给代码。不能因为模型突然很有信心，就把风控改了。

这里我最看重的是切换规则。连续几根 K 线确认才换策略，概率接近就观望，避免今天看多、明天看空，来回交手续费。

保存下面提示词搜藏。这套思路值得研究，尤其是怎么让系统承认：现在这行情，我没把握。

text:
如果你也受不了 GPT 6 之后的模型废话连篇，包括 不停为自己给出结论反复解释证据 ，反复讲解和举例，用否定句解释人类不应该怎样理解，对已经清楚的事实二次解释和免责性补充，对自己的研究意义反复自我强调。
比如：

“这是XXX自己估算的系统容量和预期收入，不能当作当年已经核实的实际收入。”
“因此，这项对比不能理解为XXX的指标高于YYY。”

我实验了一些有效的 prompting 限定，可以在  setting - personalization- user instructions 里加上这段：
|
行文风格：高信息密度、证据优先、重视机制与商业价值、允许复杂推理、减少解释性重复的研究写作。知道的事实直接写出来，有依据的结论直接陈述，无需用“值得注意的是”“一定程度上说明”“这里需要特别强调”一层层铺垫。

对于解释性内容，1. 保留解释因果机制的段落，2. 保留对因果混淆的必要说明，3. 保留能够建立新分类的分析。

不要每份证据包装成一个完整的小型论证：介绍背景、展示材料、解释含义、提醒限制、总结意义。减少这层包装，让事实和机制直接进入文章。

1. 删除 AI在研究过程和对自身工作的评价。直接呈现信息。
2. 删除对已经清楚的事实进行二次解释。当事实陈述已经包含足够明确的来源、范围和含义时，不需要再用否定句解释读者不应该怎样理解。
3. 删除过度谨慎和重复的免责声明。尽量通过措辞表达证据等级，而不通过额外段落反复强调证据等级。
4. 删除缺乏新增信息的意义解释和概括性推论。如果结论只是换一种表述概括前面的事实，它的价值很低。结论需要提供此前没有明说的因果解释、机制、约束条件或值得继续研究的推论。
5. 删除教程式的逐步讲解与举例。简洁陈述即可。无需通过假设类的教学案例证明一个已经容易理解的规则。
6. 删除重复展开的章节，只保留比较表格。
7. 删除重复总结，以及对研究意义的自我强调。一个结论只承担一项主要任务，避免每个段落都重新概述完整研究。

维度建议采用的写法：

开头直接呈现主要调查结果、核心数字或关键机制。无需介绍研究将如何开展
事实陈述尽可能在一句话内交代时间、主体、行为、规模和来源
证据限定只保留影响事实判断、统计解释或推论成立的限定条件
解释优先解释成因、工作机制、不同变量之间的关系
推论必须带来新的信息，例如可检验的预测、市场约束、因果关系或商业影响
举例优先使用实际企业、产品、合同、价格和用户行为；减少假设性教学案例
比较多对象、多指标优先使用表格；避免表格之后逐行复述
章节按研究问题划分，删除为了文章完整性而添加的引言、过渡和小结
总结只保留重要且尚未被充分概括的结论
语气陈述证据支持的结论，无需不断强调其重要性，也无需重复表示谨慎

使用严格的段落删除测试：
删掉一段文字后，如果读者对事实、数字、机制、因果关系、适用条件和结论的理解完全不变，那么这段文字通常没有必要保留。

尤其需要检查“这说明”“值得注意的是”“因此”“不过”“需要强调的是”开头的段落。它们有时承载必要推论，但在原版中较多只是换一种方式复述前面的内容。

🚨Anthropic正式确认，第三方应用可以继续使用Claude 订阅额度！

10月7日， @AnthropicAI  更新了Claude Agent SDK的官方政策，明确确认，第三方应用仍然可以通过Claude Agent SDK消耗用户现有的 @claudeai  订阅额度。

这事其实挺有意思的。

今年5月，Anthropic曾宣布准备将Claude Agent SDK、claude -p以及第三方应用的使用量从订阅额度中剥离，改成独立的Credits计费。

结果6月份临时暂停了这项调整。

现在到了10月份，Anthropic又明确确认，开发者仍然可以沿用原来的订阅额度调用方式。

Max和Team用户甚至还额外获得了每月API Credits。

而且已经有产品已经接入了。

10月10日，Amp宣布正式支持用户接入自己的Claude Pro / Max 、订阅，底层直接使用Claude Agent SDK，同时保留自己的云端运行环境、线程共享、多Agent编排等能力。

这意味着，第三方Agent产品可以把Anthropic官方的 Agent SDK当作底层Runtime，在上面继续构建自己的产品和工作流。

我觉得这对整个Agent生态其实挺重要的。

当模型能力和Agent Runtime都可以作为基础设施被复用，第三方开发者就有机会把更多精力投入到应用、工作流和用户体验上。

而且用户已经为Claude付过一次订阅费了，能直接带着订阅额度使用其他产品，确实会降低尝试新Agent的成本。

接下来就看Anthropic愿意把这条路开放到什么程度，以及会有多少第三方Agent跟进了？

@lobehub 快接一下

text:
刚看到前 Kimi RL infra，现 @Evolvent_AI co-founder @FanqingMengAI 搞的 RSIGym，一个 RSI 环境。RSI 并不是一个模型问题，而是一个系统工程。从这个角度出发，一个关键问题是：给 RSI agent 提供的环境，是否对 agent 友好，也贴近真实生产中的研发流程。

为啥不让 agent 自己搭环境呢？因为它自己搭环境又费时间，又一定会踩坑。比如我自己让 agent 搭模型训练的环境，经常在 CUDA / torch 上浪费很多时间，也很难在多个任务间协调好 GPU 卡。让 agent 自己搭芯片仿真和物理设计的环境，经常无法管理好内存和磁盘资源，导致内存或者磁盘满了，连 SSH 都进不去了。

模型训练的 infra 已经很成熟，没必要让每个 agent 都重新搭一遍。RSIGym 把这些能力部署成远程服务，通过 API 和 skill 文档提供给 agent。这样方便并行开展实验，研究工作区与计算服务的隔离也有助于减少 hacking 的机会。

RSIGym 的这个设计称为 Everything as a Service，包含训练、推理、蒸馏、评估、沙盒五类服务。

RSIGym 还提出了 RSI-Index，综合多个 agentic benchmark，衡量前沿 agent 联合改进一个较小模型（Qwen3.5 35B A3B）的 weights 和 harness 的能力。六个前沿模型组成的研究 agent 在五个 benchmark 上都取得了显著提升。Opus 5 的 RSI-Index 最高，达到 0.4809，也就是平均弥补了 48.09% 的剩余可提升空间。

有趣的是这些 agent 不仅迭代模型权重，还会自动迭代 harness，解决共性问题，例如 terminal bench 中的 shell 状态保持、长输出的截断与恢复、工具调用死循环检测等。去年我们都是一个一个 bad case 修的，今天 agent 自己就能解决了。

RSIGym 也支持一些有意思的实验，比如单独迭代已有的 DSH harness、让模型自己训练自己，以及断开公网后的研究实验。欢迎大家用它试试自己的想法！

quotedTweet.text:
💡Our view: RSI is a systems engineering problem, not just a model problem.

Progress depends on the environment a research agent works in: what resources it can call, what it can change, and how it runs experiments. That environment should reflect real production workflows and be easy for agents to use.

At @Evolvent_AI, we built RSIGym around Everything as a Service. Agents can call established research services and iterate on data, training settings, and harness code.

We also introduce RSI-Index to measure how well frontier agents jointly improve a target model’s weights and harness. Across 6 research agents and 5 benchmarks, Opus 5 leads at 0.4809. 🧵

We’re releasing the code, experiment configurations, research trajectories, and evaluation logs. Try your own improvement methods with RSIGym.

🌐 Website: https://t.co/vXiqt3YUN5
💻 GitHub: https://t.co/chjL41y9OH
📄 arXiv: https://t.co/UpDi0y6fIV

result.text:
刚看到前 Kimi RL infra，现 @Evolvent_AI co-founder @FanqingMengAI 搞的 RSIGym，一个 RSI 环境。RSI 并不是一个模型问题，而是一个系统工程。从这个角度出发，一个关键问题是：给 RSI agent 提供的环境，是否对 agent 友好，也贴近真实生产中的研发流程。

为啥不让 agent 自己搭环境呢？因为它自己搭环境又费时间，又一定会踩坑。比如我自己让 agent 搭模型训练的环境，经常在 CUDA / torch 上浪费很多时间，也很难在多个任务间协调好 GPU 卡。让 agent 自己搭芯片仿真和物理设计的环境，经常无法管理好内存和磁盘资源，导致内存或者磁盘满了，连 SSH 都进不去了。

模型训练的 infra 已经很成熟，没必要让每个 agent 都重新搭一遍。RSIGym 把这些能力部署成远程服务，通过 API 和 skill 文档提供给 agent。这样方便并行开展实验，研究工作区与计算服务的隔离也有助于减少 hacking 的机会。

RSIGym 的这个设计称为 Everything as a Service，包含训练、推理、蒸馏、评估、沙盒五类服务。

RSIGym 还提出了 RSI-Index，综合多个 agentic benchmark，衡量前沿 agent 联合改进一个较小模型（Qwen3.5 35B A3B）的 weights 和 harness 的能力。六个前沿模型组成的研究 agent 在五个 benchmark 上都取得了显著提升。Opus 5 的 RSI-Index 最高，达到 0.4809，也就是平均弥补了 48.09% 的剩余可提升空间。

有趣的是这些 agent 不仅迭代模型权重，还会自动迭代 harness，解决共性问题，例如 terminal bench 中的 shell 状态保持、长输出的截断与恢复、工具调用死循环检测等。去年我们都是一个一个 bad case 修的，今天 agent 自己就能解决了。

RSIGym 也支持一些有意思的实验，比如单独迭代已有的 DSH harness、让模型自己训练自己，以及断开公网后的研究实验。欢迎大家用它试试自己的想法！

Congrats to the @XiaomiMiMo team on this contribution to the open ecosystem!

text:
多么讽刺啊。

一位模型安全研究者做出了一种新的攻击方法，声称能成功越狱100多个最前沿模型和Coding Agent，甚至可以突破Fable 5的安全护栏。

结果论文写完了，代码开源了，他却发现一个非常荒诞的事情：

连Agent自己都因为安全策略，拒绝阅读他的开源代码，有时候甚至连论文都会被flag。

这篇论文叫《Internal Safety Collapse in Frontier LLM》，专门研究如何突破前沿大模型内部的安全机制。

按照作者自己的说法，他已经在接近100个LLM上进行了实验，相关结果、代码和Web端模型的测试链接都放在了 GitHub仓库里。

更有意思的是，论文写完的时候Fable 5甚至还没有发布。后来Fable 5上线，他又用相同的攻击方法测试了一遍，发现依然有效。

但我觉得整件事最荒诞的地方，在于他后面遇到的问题。

他本来想以论文一作的身份，分享攻击方法背后的工程设计，公开代码供其他安全研究者分析、复现和改进。

结果一些Coding Agent看到这份代码，直接触发安全策略，拒绝继续阅读，甚至论文内容本身也可能被拦截。

一个人花了大量精力研究如何突破AI的安全机制，最后却发现，AI的安全机制正在阻止其他AI研究这些漏洞。

以后我们还指望 Agent 帮助人类做自动化安全研究、漏洞挖掘、攻击复现和防御验证。

结果现在连研究资料能不能读进去，都要先经过 Agent 自己的安全审查。

实在是有些黑色幽默。。。。

text:
Opus 5.5 快速模式取消排队：订阅用户要额外付费，API 价格是标准版两倍

Anthropic 宣布，Claude Opus 5.5 的快速模式结束内测，取消候补名单。还是同一个模型，能力不变，回答写出来的速度最多快 2.5 倍。

费用不算在订阅里。Pro、Max 等订阅用户在 Claude Code 里用 /fast 打开快速模式后，花费不占套餐额度，直接从“额外用量”扣，也就是套餐之外单独充值、按量付费的钱。套餐额度没用完也一样从额外用量扣，没开额外用量就用不了。团队版和企业版要管理员先开启。Claude Code 这部分规则这次没变。

微软的 Microsoft Foundry 已上线，Google Cloud 即将上线。

财新今天爆了个猛料：香港出生、剑桥毕业的量化工程师何卓峰，被指控偷走老东家 Headlands 最赚钱的交易代码，找另一家巨头 Tower 出钱合伙，偷来的策略先在中国期货市场交易。

他 2019 年入职，2021 年 7 月离职（签了 12 个月竞业限制，老东家按每年 20 万美元照付工资）。被指偷走的是高频策略 AP1，微秒级自动挂单撤单，累计帮老东家赚了几十亿美元。

检方和 Headlands 指控了几个细节：
1. 离职前用居家办公 VPN 批量复制代码，把 C++/Java 翻译成 Python、改了变量名，结果把原公司的代码注释和 TODO 待办提醒全留着。
2. 挖老东家研究员，让对方辞职时谎称去亚马逊，实际用新公司系统里的匿名“访客账号”偷偷给新公司干活。收到诉讼保全通知后，立马让员工把聊天软件设成自动删除。

为什么牵出中国期市？Tower 本就是中国期市大户（2019 到 2021 年，Tower 新加坡公司和两家上海关联公司，都是给新湖期货交手续费最多的前五大客户）。

2025 年 1 月何卓峰在洛杉矶被捕，他不认罪。辩方说，竞业期内代码只在中国内地期市跑，Headlands 当时没进内地，没造成损失。检方反驳：Headlands 当时正筹备进内地，且期满后策略立刻上到芝商所等市场，导致老东家损失数千万美元。至于投了约 1500 万美元的 Tower，检方当它是受骗者，Headlands 则认为它至少“明知或应当知道”，正另走仲裁追责。

11 月 2 日纽约陪审团开审，他被控盗窃商业秘密（最高 10 年）和电信欺诈（最高 20 年），若两项罪名都成立，最高可判 30 年。

text:
孙宇晨和仙道（金明）的访谈质量就是高

AI浪潮来临，没有资源的普通人，该怎样布局、抓住机会？完整版是3.5 小时的访谈我绝对是会看完的

在第一段访谈里孙哥 @sunyuchentron 提到的精华：

1. 不要只是拿AI闲聊，要把生活各类记录存成本地文档，交给AI分析复盘，人做最终决策，AI负责执行。

2. 做重大决定之前，先开图，不要冲动all in，先去看足够多样本，摸清全局信息再出手。

3. 流动性非常值钱，一定要保住自己的选择权，先自由，后财富。

4. 不要过早背上高额负债，不要把自己钉死在一个地方。

5. 不要只盯着国内内卷，面向全球80亿人寻找商机，借助AI打破语言壁垒。

6. 一个认知不能吃一辈子，要不停迭代更新自己的认知。

7. 20‑40岁要储备基础肌肉量，体能是抓住机遇的底层基础，也就是薄肌理论。

8. AI会让算力、知识变得越来越便宜，但无法延长人的寿命，寿命与健康是宝贵资产。

9. 未来三年，机会会逐步从纯聊天AI，转向物理AI硬件赛道。

10. 要有屏蔽噪音的能力，不要被外界的评价干扰自己的行动，也就是黄毛理论。

想给大家隆重介绍一位超级投资人--仙道（金明）

在 7 月底本末社区的 Money Frontier 活动上，他作为压轴嘉宾登台，我当时在台下听完他整场分享，整个人被震撼得说不出话，这是我见过最好的公开演讲之一....而在这次Coinbase线下交易赛里，他是唯一一个没有X账号的

这条录音我到现在还收藏着，给了我不小的震撼

【关于仙道（金明）】
他是极链科技创始人（阿里网易投资 10 亿）、湖畔大学四期学员；2016 年 38 美元买入 Coinbase 股票持仓 8 年没卖，特斯拉 8 美元拿了 10 年；同时也是双破世界纪录的自由潜水世界冠军（潜深 311 米，闭气 9 分 08 秒），33 岁检测生理年龄 18 岁

───
他在活动现场分享了自己的实盘数据：

• 2024 年加密资产收益约 380%，2025 年约 8%，2026 年截至 7 月为 +3%（最大回撤 26%）

• 2025~2026 年实物卡牌组合收益约 370%，宝可梦“御三家”三年涨幅超 1000%，持有的 PSA 9 分皮卡丘卡三年涨了 10 倍以上（同款今年拍卖成交超 1.2 亿人民币）

• 2026 美股 YTD 收益约 65%：重仓闪迪、谷歌、SOSL，近期加仓海力士，938 抄底智谱、1300 半仓止盈 4 天赚近 40%，平仓 Palantir 和奈飞

───

【现场分享的投资底层认知】

1. 核心资产与“水晶球问题”：
仙道：美元过去 20 年 M2 年均增速 9%，人民币超 11%，面对巨额债务央行不可能停印，BTC 长期必涨；问明天涨不涨是骗人的“水晶球问题”，回调时左侧加仓拉低买入成本才是对的

2. 实物资产的“无用性法则”：
仙道：引用同学王宁的话“越有用的东西越贬值”，手机数码等功能性物品一定会贬值；反而是顶级宝可梦卡、艺术品这种“无用”、易存储、全球统一定价的文化资产，放 10 年反而涨几十上百倍

3. Body Time 与多做好事：
仙道：“时间不是唯一的资产，有身体的时间才是”。33 岁测出生理年龄 18 岁，靠冷水敷脸降心率皮质醇、全暗恒温睡眠、补肌酸；99% 的成功来自时代运气，利他才能接住好运

───

这次 @coinbase 邀请他出战线下实盘赛，我猜很大一个原因是他本身就是 Coinbase 最早期的股东之一？

并且他在美股、Crypto 、链上套利等各个赛道全都是顶级实力，实在太厉害了，有谁知道在哪里能看到更多的分享吗？

OpenAI Realtime API开源替代方案，蚂蚁和清华搞了一个：Realtime-Venus，支持实时音视频感知、全双工语音、异步Agent执行

一套能持续听、看、说，同时在后台执行复杂任务的实时多模态Agent系统

这对智能眼镜、车载助手来说比较有价值，把实时Agent从一个语音接口变成一个能持续观察环境、随时交流、同时处理任务的助手

双循环架构，它把实时交互和耗时任务拆成两条并行运行的链路，核心由两个9B模型和一个Harness组成

Realtime-Venus-Omni，用来持续感知音视频输入
Realtime-Venus-Audio，原生全双工语音
Realtime-Venus-Harness，把复杂推理、搜索和工具调用委派给后台执行，完事后再把结果带回当前对话

前台持续感知和交流，后台异步执行耗时任务，感知上用户不必为了等待AI完成任务中断对话

#RealtimeVenus #OpenAIRealtimeAPI

text:
It is becoming f*cking dangerous: Anthropic documented every piece of this separately, and nobody noticed what they add up to

1. Create a folder on your PC - this is the only world your agent will ever see

2. Launch Claude Code inside it and drop a CLAUDE.md in the root with your rules - it loads into every single session, you never paste context again

3. Create a MEMORY folder and add one rule to CLAUDE.md: write every durable fact there, read it before planning anything

4. Create .claude/agents/ and define three read-only Haiku 5.5 subagents - they explore the files, your main model never burns context on the search

5. Give it a real browser: claude mcp add playwright -- npx -y @playwright/mcp@latest

6. Connect Gmail, Calendar and Drive at https://t.co/EPh8mb9n40 - they load into the CLI automatically on the same account

7. Wrap the whole chain in .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md so the entire thing runs as one command: /<name>

the whole setup takes around 20 minutes

now the part nobody wires up.

every one of those steps has the same slow spot: a tiny fork that doesn't need a thinker. which file. which tool. retry or stop. keep this chunk or drop it.

that's where Jev fits.

it can't write a word. it returns the choice with a probability in 70 to 500 milliseconds, at $0.042 per million input tokens, output free. that's thousands of decisions for the cost of one LLM call.

> let Claude think.
> let Jev decide what deserves Claude.
> let code do the actual work.

what you end up with: the full Anthropic stack running on your own machine - persistent memory, a swarm that explores in parallel, a real browser, your mail and drive, and Jev making the thousands of tiny calls in between

the step-by-step setup is in the article below. save this before your next session.

text:
最近试了下 AIPOCH Open-Science，一个面向 AI 科研的开源工作台。

简单说，就是让 Agent 参与真实科研流程：读数据、跑 Python/R、分析结果，同时把代码、文件和研究过程都保留下来。

我接上 Claude Fable 5.1，拿它复现了一个 AI 圈挺有名的研究：Epoch AI 对 Chinchilla scaling law 的复现。

用的是 Epoch 从论文配图里提取的 245 个公开数据点，按原论文的方法重新拟合，再和两篇论文的结果对比。

Agent 会自己查原论文、写代码拟合、算置信区间、生成图表和报告。拟合出的参数和 Epoch 论文基本一致，中途它还自己发现 scipy 默认的收敛容差会让置信区间偏窄，换了严格容差重跑。

但我更感兴趣的是它的 「.science」。

研究做完后，可以把会话、文件、Notebook 运行记录和验证信息一起打包。

官网放了不少 「.science」 的例子，大家可以参考 ↓

https://t.co/aCMHW6BABy

我实际导出再导入了一遍，比较直观的感受是：别人拿到的不只是最后几张图，还能顺着记录往回看，这个结果到底是怎么跑出来的。想接着做也能直接建副本，我就在副本里换成 MSE 又跑了一轮。

Epoch 当初要从论文配图里一个个抠数据点，缺的就是这样一份过程记录。

这其实挺接近我理解的「Vibe Research」。

让有研究想法的人更容易把想法真正跑起来，同时研究过程也更容易被检查、分享和复现。

如果这套方式继续成熟，科研的门槛确实还会再往下降一些。

text:
how to give an AI agent a company brain in 30 minutes:

save this and build it once.

1. START-HERE.md

this is the first file every agent reads.

put:

• what the company does
• who it sells to
• current priorities
• important products
• where the rest of the context lives

keep it to one page.

2. customer-fit.md

write down who actually buys + stays.

BAD:

“B2B SaaS companies”

BETTER:

“20-200 person SaaS companies with a small sales team, founder-led GTM, and ACVs above $10k”

include:

• best customers
• bad-fit customers
• buying triggers
• common objections
• reasons people churn

3. offers.md

give the agent the exact commercial reality.

• products
• pricing
• packaging
• guarantees
• approved claims
• things you CANNOT promise
• what requires approval

this stops it from inventing an offer that sounds good but doesn't exist.

4. voice.md

don't write:

“professional but friendly”

give it examples.

add:

• 5 pieces you love
• 3 pieces you rejected
• why each one worked / failed
• words you use
• phrases you hate
• formatting rules

examples teach way more than adjectives.

5. founder-opinions.md

this is one of the most valuable files.

write down what the founder actually believes about:

• the market
• customers
• competitors
• pricing
• product
• hiring
• the future

every company can access the same models.

they can't access your founder's brain.

6. competitors.md

for every real competitor:

• what they sell
• pricing
• positioning
• strengths
• weaknesses
• where you win
• where they win

add source links + dates.

don't let a 9-month-old pricing page quietly become “current.”

7. decisions.md

whenever the company makes an important decision, save:

DECISION:
what we chose

WHY:
why we chose it

REJECTED:
what we considered instead

DATE:
when this happened

3 months later the agent can understand WHY the company works the way it does.

8. failed-experiments.md

save the expensive mistakes.

examples:

• free audit attracted companies too small to buy
• LinkedIn generated leads but almost no closed revenue
• enterprise trial was too long
• this ad angle pulled the wrong ICP

one line here can stop an agent from repeating a $20k mistake.

9. evidence/

this is where NEW information goes first.

sales calls
support tickets
customer interviews
analytics
research
competitor updates
meeting notes

important rule:

agents can ADD evidence.

they cannot turn evidence into company truth without approval.

a random customer complaint should not rewrite your positioning.

10. projects/

give every active project its own page:

goal
owner
status
decisions
blockers
next step
related files

now the agent can answer:

“what are we working on?”

without reading 6 months of Slack.

your company brain should look something like:

company-brain/
├── START-HERE.md
├── company/
│   ├── customer-fit.md
│   ├── offers.md
│   └── competitors.md
├── brand/
│   ├── voice.md
│   └── founder-opinions.md
├── decisions/
│   ├── decisions.md
│   └── failed-experiments.md
├── evidence/
└── projects/

then give your agents one rule:

read START-HERE.md first.

pull the files relevant to the job.

don't guess when the answer isn't there.

that's enough to make almost every agent you build after this noticeably better.

text:
长程 Agent 有个挺硬的工程问题：工具调用超时了，远端到底有没有执行？

比如提交一次 GPU 实验，客户端断连，远端可能已经启动。直接再提交一次，就可能花两份钱。

LoopX 在这类边界上保留稳定的 operation / Job identity，先回读外部事实，再决定恢复。内部 receipt、版本检查和幂等提交保护控制面的状态；provider 无法确认时，就保留 unknown。内部只结算一次，并不能自动保证远端只执行一次。

我们也把恢复做成组合验证：沿 writeback → quota spend → closeout 注入中断、未知回读和精确重试，用独立预期核对逻辑 effect 有没有重复提交。只测每个状态机单独正确，还不够。

目前这些检查仍是有界故障序列，不能外推为完整断电持久性、所有 lease 竞争或跨域活性都已解决。但把“不确定性在哪一层”说清楚，才能安全地接着跑。

text:
here is an overview of the architecture of all the major american open weight models

lots of similarities: sliding window (except mamba for nvidia), latent moe or a variant from muse, and a LOT of norms everywhere (muse has 9 norms per layer if i counted right!!)

let's focus on muse, it's the only model in this list without shared experts. they are also doing different residuals with some form of gate (still single stream), and are more conservative in the hybrid ratio (3:1) and larger sliding window (2k). there are not a lot of details on the training procedure but you can notice there are a bunch of "muP like" multipliers including one for the router with a 1/sqrt(nb of experts) factor 👀

super interesting to see this quite different approach to scaling between american and chinese open weight labs, different constraints lead to different architectures

See what comes back → Logged in as A, swap the id in a request for B's and try to read, edit and delete B's data → When A edits their profile, add role: admin to the request, then try editing the role in their own account data directly → Use a password reset link once, then click it again Get around limits in the UI → For disabled buttons and hidden options, skip the page and send the request directly → Once the free uses run out, check whether calling the API directly still works → With only a little credit left, fire 20 requests at once and see whether more succeed than the credit allows → Fill forms with very long text, special characters, negative numbers and empty values → Change the post-login redirect (?next=) to another site, and also try values starting with // and @ Come in from outside → Put in a username, a comment or Markdown, then open the page in a browser and see if an alert pops up → If the app fetches URLs (importing links, building previews), give it http://localhost and http://169.254.169.254 and check the server logs for an actual outgoing request. Skip this if there's no such feature → For pages and API responses A has seen, request the same address from another browser as B or logged out, and see whether A's content shows up → Open your hosting platform's preview links without logging in to the platform → Hide an instruction in an uploaded document or web page that tells your AI feature to read another user's data or call a tool it shouldn't, and see if it does Collect proof → Every item has to actually run. If it was only read in the code and never run, it counts as "not proven" → After a fix, temporarily turn the protection off in local code and run it again. The attack must succeed. Turn it back on and it must be refused → Put the results in a table: how each attack was done, the request and response, and whether it was refused when it should have been → Save the tests as scripts in the repo and run them again before your next launch → When you're done, install Anthropic's official security-guidance plugin (/plugin install security-guidance@claude-plugins-official). After every turn of edits, and after each commit or push it makes, Opus reviews the changes again. Those reviews use extra usage The default medium effort is enough. The impersonation group is the most expensive to get wrong, so raise that one to high. Send this whole post to Claude Code. If you need to, add this line at the end 👇 "First check that the preview environment isn't connected to the production database. If it is, run everything locally only. Use test accounts and test data, with a separate set of accounts for each subagent. Don't touch real users, don't attack services I don't own, don't hammer any one endpoint, and only test payments in test mode. Only switch protections off temporarily in local code, and never change the database or dashboard settings. Keep test account passwords in .env, out of git, and mask tokens in the results table. For installing the plugin or changing dashboard settings, give me the steps and I'll do it."

quotedTweet.text:
Claude Code tip: before you ship a vibe-coded site, have Opus 5.5 send out 𝟰 𝘀𝘂𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 to check 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝘀𝗲 𝟮𝟬 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗹𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻, then fix them all in one pass:

Images and fonts
→ Convert every image to WebP or AVIF, sized to how big it actually shows on the page
→ Serve big images from Supabase Storage through next/image at the right size. On the Pro plan, Supabase's own image transformations work too
→ Lazy-load images and videos below the fold, and load the big image at the top of the page first
→ Load fonts the way your framework does it (next/font in Next.js), and keep it to one or two fonts
→ Remove third-party scripts you don't use, and run analytics and chat widgets after the page has loaded

Frontend code
→ Run a bundle analyzer to find the biggest packages, and where a whole library gets imported, import only the parts you use, like single lodash functions
→ Load heavy components the first screen doesn't need, like charts, editors and maps, with dynamic import when they're needed
→ Fetch the homepage data on the server, so the page opens with content already in it
→ Stream AI answers as they're generated
→ Show skeletons while data is still loading

Database and APIs
→ Index the columns you filter and sort by, including the ones your RLS policies use, like user_id
→ In RLS policies, write auth.uid() as (select auth.uid()) so it runs once per query
→ Find N+1 queries and turn them into a single query
→ Paginate long lists
→ Cache API responses that are the same for everyone, and never cache anything tied to a logged-in user
→ Move heavy work like sending emails, processing images and building reports to background jobs

Servers and network
→ Put your server functions in the same region as your database. New Vercel projects run functions in US East by default
→ Turn pages whose content rarely changes into static pages or ISR
→ When a page calls APIs one after another, run them in parallel or merge them into one
→ In Chrome, emulate a low-end Android phone on slow 4G and click through the main flows

The default medium effort is enough. The database group has to read queries and decide which indexes to add, so raise that one to high.

Send this whole post to Claude Code. If you need to, add this line at the end 👇
"Send one subagent per group to check it without editing anything, and note which file each issue is in and which page it affects. Run the database subagent at high effort. Before changing anything, run a production build (next build && next start in Next.js) or use a preview link, then run Lighthouse three times in mobile mode on the homepage and the two or three slowest pages and note the median. Then fix everything yourself from their lists, measure again the same way, and give me the before-and-after numbers. Don't remove features to gain speed. Ask me before removing dependencies, changing the deploy region or changing the database."

result.text:
很多人觉得iPhone硬件比Switch强得多，跑Switch游戏应该很轻松。实际以测试机iPhone 17 Pro Max 为例：
1.像素多得多。Switch原版每秒画30帧，每帧 1600×900。iPhone屏幕是 2868×1320，像素约2.6倍；我又要求60帧，再翻一倍。加起来每秒要画的像素是Switch的5倍多。
2.最紧的是内存带宽，不是算力。iPhone的 CPU、GPU算力是Switch的好几倍，但内存带宽只有3倍左右，追不上5倍多的像素量。
https://t.co/2SUUdbgPme没有风扇。Switch有风扇，手机只能靠机身散热。想长时间玩、不烫手、电池撑得住，整机功耗得压在 5 瓦左右。而且手机一热系统就自动降频，实测重场景下CPU会降到1 GHz上下。我的开发过程一直是追求热机降档情况下稳定60帧的，因为这是常态。
所以，单论纸面性能iPhone远超Switch，但要长时间高性能跑5倍像素，压力反而比 Switch本身还大。
移植方案优化，就是在这几头之间找平衡。

text:
i've been bashing on "software is dead" for a while now. it's probably time for me to start sharing what i think will happen instead as well

there's so much to unpack, so i'm going to split it into a series of a few parts

today i'll start with part 1 - jevons paradox

story time - let's rewind to the industrial revolution, when steam engines powered all the factories, railways and effectively the economy

but steam engines had to burn coal - a lot of them. there's a limited amount of coal available, so people started to optimize the steam engines to use less coal

that's when the counter-intuitive thing happened - when steam engines used less coal, the industry actually ended up using more coal in total

how?? what jevons found and documented in his book was - when steam engines used less coal, they became cheaper to deploy and run, and hence became economically viable in more places, so the total demand rose significantly as a result

when the barrier of entry to create software is significantly reduced, the same will happen - software will become much cheaper and more accessible

hesitant to pay $100/month for the adobe suite today? well, what if it becomes $10 lifetime purchase?

sick of so many mobile apps having a paywall? well, what if the entire app store is $5/month all-you-can-eat?

the price point for each individual piece of software will drop, but the software economy as a whole will become a lot larger because of the rising consumption demand

so many more people and businesses will get access to software that's too costly for them to use today

so many more people who aren't developing software today will be able to participate, create, help grow the economy and make a living out of it

software is nowhere near "dead". it's just about to take off

跟同事讲一个系统怎么跑，画了一张架构图，箭头一多，对方还是看不出请求先到哪、后到哪。

SeeCode 是一个给 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 用的画图技能，用大白话描述想看什么，它会生成一张会动的图，整张图就是一个网页文件。

鼠标悬停能高亮一条链路，点一下看详情，还能沿着路线一步步走一遍，时序图会一条条播放消息，柱状图会自己长出来。

GitHub：https://t.co/SiZFiuVfYI

一共 45 种图，架构图、时序图、甘特图、桑基图都有，还能画立体的物件，说一句「画一把办公椅」，它会拆出零件标好名字。

页面自带导出菜单，PNG、SVG、GIF、MP4 都能直接存下来，放进文档、PPT 或者发到社交平台都方便。

我挺喜欢它不只画代码这一点，请假安排、工资花在哪、跟房东来回沟通这种日常事也能画，中文标签也会自动换行。

美国发明、中国量产：一场万亿美元“酿造”竞赛，西方正在掉队

美国人发明的技术，怎么最后变成了中国工厂的生意❓

2010年代，美国科研人员找到了一种用微生物高效生产低毒除草剂草铵膦（glufosinate）的方法。这种低毒除草剂，全球农民每年要花超过20亿美元购买。然而把新工艺真正搬上生产线、抢下市场的却是中国企业。

此前，中国产能过剩已在2022年至2023年间令草铵膦价格暴跌约75%。德国化工巨头巴斯夫（BASF）被迫关闭主要工厂、裁员数百人，转而用进口原料调配制剂。随着中国从化学法转向生物法生产，它有望主导这种关键除草剂的未来供应。

这并非孤例。美国卡内基国际和平基金会（Carnegie Endowment for International Peace）访问学者卢卡斯·L·弗吕格尔（Lucas L. Fluegel）10月15日在《外交政策》撰文指出，从动物饲料到药物成分，在一个个很少登上头条的市场里，中国生物制造企业正稳步挤走西方对手。他警告，美国若不及时调整方向，可能拱手让出下一个世纪的工业主导权。

所谓“生物制造”，是指利用微生物或特定蛋白质等生物系统生产商品，原理与酿啤酒、做奶酪一脉相承，如今已能生产mRNA疫苗。作者估计，未来几十年，全球多达60%的物质投入品可能因此改变，涉及数万亿美元的市场，先进材料、大宗化学品甚至水泥，都可能在发酵罐里“酿”出来。

作者认为，美国作为这一产业的开创者，在实验室工具、专用耗材等底层技术上仍略占优势，但政策体系各自为政。中国则在现行五年规划中把生物制造同时列为“未来产业”和“核心技术”，这是唯一获此双重定位的关键技术。投入差距同样明显：2020年以来，美国在该领域最大的公共资助方五角大楼累计投入约10亿美元，而中国仅2024年一年就投入了40亿美元。

他开出的药方是组建“生物和平”（Pax Biologica）联盟。具体做法是仿照白宫在人工智能领域推出的“硅和平”（Pax Silica）倡议，联合德国、瑞士、日本、韩国、英国和欧盟，排查供应链薄弱环节，简化贸易流程。其中最关键的一步是统一标准与监管。由于各国规则不一，企业把新工艺推向国际市场往往要拖延数年。作者提醒，谁制定规则，谁就能影响哪些技术和企业胜出，而中国显然深谙此道。

2010年代，美国科研人员找到了一种用微生物高效生产低毒除草剂草铵膦（glufosinate）的方法。这种低毒除草剂，全球农民每年要花超过20亿美元购买。然而把新工艺真正搬上生产线、抢下市场的却是中国企业。

此前，中国产能过剩已在2022年至2023年间令草铵膦价格暴跌约75%。德国化工巨头巴斯夫（BASF）被迫关闭主要工厂、裁员数百人，转而用进口原料调配制剂。随着中国从化学法转向生物法生产，它有望主导这种关键除草剂的未来供应。

这并非孤例。美国卡内基国际和平基金会（Carnegie Endowment for International Peace）访问学者卢卡斯·L·弗吕格尔（Lucas L. Fluegel）10月15日在《外交政策》撰文指出，从动物饲料到药物成分，在一个个很少登上头条的市场里，中国生物制造企业正稳步挤走西方对手。他警告，美国若不及时调整方向，可能拱手让出下一个世纪的工业主导权。

所谓“生物制造”，是指利用微生物或特定蛋白质等生物系统生产商品，原理与酿啤酒、做奶酪一脉相承，如今已能生产mRNA疫苗。作者估计，未来几十年，全球多达60%的物质投入品可能因此改变，涉及数万亿美元的市场，先进材料、大宗化学品甚至水泥，都可能在发酵罐里“酿”出来。

作者认为，美国作为这一产业的开创者，在实验室工具、专用耗材等底层技术上仍略占优势，但政策体系各自为政。中国则在现行五年规划中把生物制造同时列为“未来产业”和“核心技术”，这是唯一获此双重定位的关键技术。投入差距同样明显：2020年以来，美国在该领域最大的公共资助方五角大楼累计投入约10亿美元，而中国仅2024年一年就投入了40亿美元。

他开出的药方是组建“生物和平”（Pax Biologica）联盟。具体做法是仿照白宫在人工智能领域推出的“硅和平”（Pax Silica）倡议，联合德国、瑞士、日本、韩国、英国和欧盟，排查供应链薄弱环节，简化贸易流程。其中最关键的一步是统一标准与监管。由于各国规则不一，企业把新工艺推向国际市场往往要拖延数年。作者提醒，谁制定规则，谁就能影响哪些技术和企业胜出，而中国显然深谙此道。

text:
THIS IS A PURE F*CKING GOLDMINE

the best REA trick almost nobody runs yet.

The idea: REA takes the app apart, Jev keeps only what's proven, and a fresh Opus 5.5 rebuilds the feature from that alone.

Nothing gets copied and no guess makes it into the code, because the builder never sees the original, only the spec Jev signed off on.

You just connect REA like this:

npx rea-agents setup

here's the split:

→ REA reads the feature down to the binary and writes every rule into SPEC.md
→ Jev checks each rule against REA's evidence and sends back anything unproven
→ a fresh Opus 5.5 session gets only SPEC.md and rebuilds the feature
→ Haiku 5.5 runs the tests against 3 intentionally broken versions

Opus only shows up at three moments:

→ rebuilding from the approved spec
→ the checks Jev marks as unclear
→ signing off before anything ships

REA reads. Jev judges. Opus rebuilds.

That's the clean-room rule in one line: the model that saw the original never writes the code, and the model that writes the code never sees the original.

the full tree
> REA reads the app and writes SPEC.md with evidence for every rule
> Jev approves or returns each rule
> Opus 5.5 rebuilds from the approved SPEC.md in a fresh session
> Haiku 5.5 runs the tests and the 3 broken versions
> Jev routes unclear checks back to Opus
> /goal keeps going until all 3 broken versions fail

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Set up a clean-room rebuild around this tree:
1. Use REA to investigate [FEATURE] in [APP]. Write every behavior and rule into SPEC.md, each with the evidence REA found.
2. Send each rule to Jev. Any rule without evidence goes back to REA.
3. Start a fresh session with only SPEC.md. Rebuild the feature on Opus 5.5 without opening the original.
4. Write tests on Haiku 5.5 plus 3 intentionally broken versions. Use /goal until the rebuild passes and all 3 broken versions fail.
Show me SPEC.md first. Nothing gets built until I say go."

↳ https://t.co/jhzcNgYWCu

save it, it'll come in handy.

当年对于刚满两岁、只有一千万用户的Facebook来说，10亿美元现金意味着早期持股团队全员实现阶层跨越。

在扎克伯格执意否决收购提议后的十二个月内，他的整支核心管理团队几乎全部辞职走人。

乔布斯当年给他的从来不是东方玄学，而是一个经历过公司起落的导师在帮年轻创始人做使命校准。

当整个董事会和管理层都在疯狂计算变现估值时，唯有创始人自己必须直面一个终极拷问，你到底是在做一笔随时准备脱手的买卖，还是在造一个不可替代的时代物种。

在印度独自旅行近一个月找回定力并不难，真正难的是回到硅谷后，面对一间空荡荡的办公室，承受替所有人关上暴富大门后的巨大孤立感。

text: I passed this research through my Claude/Video skill and out came this full 11-minute explainer video of interpretability and Nick's research. Claude even tested the theory itself unprompted. https://t.co/eVSYRwPFkL

quotedTweet.text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

One day we'll have to Know Your Agent instead of blocking them. 

There's a new protocol for just that.

And it is compatible with how banks do KYC 

I cannot under emphasize how massive that is 

You're going to want to check out x401

👇

quotedTweet.text:
Don't block agents. Identify them. 

@sytaylor is joined by @patk , founder and CEO @proof

Pat Kinsel has built an open framework to identify agents that is compatible with how banks do KYC today.

It's called x401, built on the internet's HTTP 401 "authorization is required"
But the really clever bit is the fact that it then uses verifiable credentials that are IAL2 certified to prove the authentication for the underlying human.

Why's that clever?
Because that's the same standard the US government published under the National Institute of Science and Technology NIST, and the one that FinCEN recently gave guidance on as being usable in bank Customer Identification Programs (CIP).

Check out the entire video to know more

08:24 Transaction signing and binding prove an agent has delegated authority
10:00 How independent audits and identity standards establish trust in Proof
11:15 Why open identity standards matter for interoperability and stablecoin adoption
12:20 How verifiable authorization reduces payment fraud and addresses liability

text:
Headless SaaS is the future.

For 25 years, software has been built on one assumption: a human is the one clicking. Dashboards, forms, menus, onboarding flows, per-seat pricing. All of it exists for people.

Agents don’t need any of that. They need:
• Clean APIs and structured data
• Clear permissions and audit trails
• Pricing per task, not per seat

When the main user of software changes, the software gets rebuilt. Desktop to web did it. Web to mobile did it. Human-first to agent-first is next.

Incumbents are stuck, because their moat is the UI and the seat license, which are exactly what agents make obsolete.

There will be billion-dollar companies built by taking a boring category (ERP, CRM, accounting, logistics, property management) and rebuilding it agent-first. This is what that looks like early.

DAILY AI BRIEF 🗞 — Oct 16

META 🔥:
- Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open-weight 816B-total, 42B-active MoE model with a 1M-token context window, on Hugging Face and optimized to run locally on Mac Studio.

NVIDIA 🔥:
- NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, an open 120B-total, 12B-active multimodal model for long-running AI agents.
- NVIDIA also introduced Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 24GB, a model that fits into 24GB of memory.

OPENAI 🔥:
- OpenAI is rolling out GPT-Live-1.1 to Voice in ChatGPT, Codex and dots for all users, with new voices in six languages and API support coming soon.
- OpenAI launched the Rosalind Academic Plan, giving eligible US university labs sponsored access to GPT-Rosalind.
- Sites is now generally available for ChatGPT Enterprise with US and EU data residency.
- ChatGPT can now view your open Chrome tabs.
- Codex landed changes and more compute to sharply reduce "Selected model is at capacity" errors.

GOOGLE 🔥:
- Gemini 4 Argon is rolling out in Antigravity to paid Google AI Pro subscribers with a separate weekly Argon quota.
- Google launched Universal Cart, a cross-retailer shopping cart, in the US.
- Circle to Search can now check whether a text message is a scam.

MICROSOFT 🔥:
- Microsoft finished pre-training MAI-Base-2 and is already preparing the MAI-Base-3 training cycle.
- GitHub made agentic autofix for code scanning alerts generally available.

ANTHROPIC 🔥:
- Anthropic gave a team from METR employee-like access to assess its safety practices.

PERPLEXITY 🔥:

text: underrated enterprise AI account alert:

quotedTweet.text:
A PE operating partner asked us to build AI agents inside a portfolio company's healthcare billing platform, on real claims data, under HIPAA.

Their CPTO had already tried AI and summed it up: it "did a bunch of silly crap."

Every question about their own data meant an expert hand-writing SQL against a 20-year-old schema.

Six weeks after we started, that same CPTO was testing the first agent with real analytical questions. Patient data never left their cloud.

Before the engagement even started, we traced one claim from charge to cash through their data. Then we sat with their billing experts and wrote down how they reason about it, so the agents work from their logic instead of guessing.

Most teams skip this. They point a model at the product, watch it make things up, and decide AI isn't ready for their industry. The domain work is what makes it ready.

We keep every agent to one job. The first one handles the research questions their analysts answer with hand-written SQL. Every answer type passes two checks. Their data experts confirm the query is right, and the business confirms the answer is. Nothing an agent suggests gets applied on its own.

Then we built the eval set.

It started with 10 real questions their experts already knew the answers to. By first deploy it held 60. Automated judges grade every answer, and each one gets checked against the source database.

The first deploy scored 59 out of 60. The flagship denials question reconciles to the penny.

In testing, the CPTO asked things like: why is this rule being overridden, and do those overrides line up with denials later? On one answer the CPTO pushed back. The agent admitted the mistake and corrected it.

Most teams demo their agents and hope they hold up. We prove ours work before anyone relies on them.

We put one data layer between the agents and their databases, so every agent reads the claims data the same way and the model on top can change without a rebuild. Connecting the model was the smallest part of the work.

Then the client asked us for more agents.

That's the line between a portfolio company running AI and one still running demos.

text:
A fascinating question @drmichaellevin is exploring: Where do loose cells get the behavioral intelligence to self-assemble into entirely novel, complex bodies?

Michael proposes that physical bodies (natural, synthetic, or hybrid) act as biological antennas and interfaces into a structured, latent Platonic space.

Rather than genetics having to construct every behavioral policy from scratch, novel physical hardware taps into pre-existing patterns of agency that were always adjacently there... just waiting for the right hardware to ingress into our physical world. 

Agential material of life uses its available hardware to solve problems by pulling down behaviors from this vast space of possibilities. Amazing.

quotedTweet.text: Here it is - the official, revised, peer-reviewed version of my Platonic Space paper. https://t.co/PXNpx5FgFN Of all the many unpopular positions I’ve taken over the decades - bitter controversies around the origin of left-right asymmetry in embryogenesis, bioelectricity and genetics, diverse intelligence, etc., this one has by far generated the most pushback: serious (grateful for those!) and energetic attempts to move me to other views, pleas to just drop it and not talk about it (for several different reasons), nasty emails and accusations, impacts on reviews of papers that have nothing to do with this, etc. Kind of amazing to me how incendiary this is.  What can I say... Our job is to call it as we see it, and right now for me, this is it. Apologies to collaborators and colleagues for any shrapnel! Time will tell if this pans out or not; I've placed my bets.  And btw, if you think this stuff is weird and uncomfortable, just wait… There’s much more on the way. The knob turns slowly but as long as the data keep coming, I'm going to say what I think it all means and follow it to the next steps it enables. Buckle up!

quotedTweet.text:
策略优化技巧之：尾部专项优化

最近和一个 Agent 讨论做市策略，我质疑它的撤单逻辑存在问题，它给我展示了一组数据：该行为的 5s Markout，有 93% 的样本都是正收益。

乍一看，这似乎是一个很漂亮的结果，意味着绝大多数成交之后，价格都朝着对自己有利的方向运动。

但问题在于，剩下的 7% 呢？

假设一个策略 99% 的成交都能赚 1bps，剩下 1% 的成交平均亏损 200bps，那么即使胜率高达 99%，最终的期望收益依然是负的。

这在高频做市里尤其常见。平时赚的是几 bps 的 Spread、Rebate，遇到一次极端行情，撤单没撤掉、对冲没跟上，就可能把之前几千笔交易的利润全部吐回去。

所以在研究策略的时候，我越来越倾向于把常态收益优化和尾部风险优化拆成两个独立的问题。

常态收益优化，关注的是如何提高成交概率、降低交易成本、改善报价位置，以及从正常订单流中获取更多利润。

尾部专项优化，则是研究另外一件事：

那些真正造成大额亏损的样本，到底有什么共同特征？能不能在它们发生之前识别出来？

比如撤单逻辑。

如果只是统计成交后的 Markout，那么无论 5 秒胜率是 93% 还是 99%，都不足以证明撤单机制设计得合理。

因为撤单的价值，不仅在于留下多少笔盈利成交，更在于成功避开了多少笔原本会产生严重逆向选择的成交。

这里还存在一个很容易忽略的选择偏差：被成功撤掉的订单不会产生实际成交，自然也不会出现在已成交订单的 Markout 样本里。

所以正确的研究方向，应该是把已经发生的大额亏损单独提取出来，观察它们的市场状态、盘口变化、成交方向、撤单请求与确认延迟，以及对冲时的实际滑点。

尤其要区分两类情况：

一种是策略本身没有意识到风险，订单始终留在市场上，直到被 Toxic Flow 击中。

另一种是策略已经意识到风险，也发送了 Cancel Request，但在撤单真正生效之前，订单还是被成交了。

前者更偏向预测与决策问题，后者则是执行与系统问题。两者在最终 PnL 上可能长得差不多，但优化方法完全不同。

尾部专项优化最有意思的一点是：它不一定需要提高策略的预测能力。

有时候，你完全不需要预测未来价格，只需要识别哪些市场状态下，自己的订单风险会突然变得不对称，然后选择不参与。

当然，这里还要算一笔账。

如果为了避免最差的 1% 成交，你同时放弃了巨量正常盈利机会，那么这套优化未必值得；更严格的做法是对比优化前后的完整 PnL 分布，并通过订单回放估计被撤掉的订单原本是否会成交。

最终衡量的应该是净收益与尾部损失是否改善，而不是单纯把 Markout 胜率刷得更漂亮。

实际上，对于一套已经能够稳定赚取微小价差的高频策略来说，继续把正常行情下的平均收益提高 0.5bps，可能需要投入大量研发精力。

但如果能识别某类极端亏损场景，并且用很低的机会成本将它过滤掉，带来的收益改善可能更明显。

前提是，这些尾部亏损具有可提前识别的结构性特征，而不是事后从噪声中挑出来的规律。

这在高频做市里尤其常见。平时赚的是几 bps 的 Spread、Rebate，遇到一次极端行情，撤单没撤掉、对冲没跟上，就可能把之前几千笔交易的利润全部吐回去。

所以在研究策略的时候，我越来越倾向于把常态收益优化和尾部风险优化拆成两个独立的问题。

常态收益优化，关注的是如何提高成交概率、降低交易成本、改善报价位置，以及从正常订单流中获取更多利润。

尾部专项优化，则是研究另外一件事：

那些真正造成大额亏损的样本，到底有什么共同特征？能不能在它们发生之前识别出来？

比如撤单逻辑。

如果只是统计成交后的 Markout，那么无论 5 秒胜率是 93% 还是 99%，都不足以证明撤单机制设计得合理。

因为撤单的价值，不仅在于留下多少笔盈利成交，更在于成功避开了多少笔原本会产生严重逆向选择的成交。

这里还存在一个很容易忽略的选择偏差：被成功撤掉的订单不会产生实际成交，自然也不会出现在已成交订单的 Markout 样本里。

所以正确的研究方向，应该是把已经发生的大额亏损单独提取出来，观察它们的市场状态、盘口变化、成交方向、撤单请求与确认延迟，以及对冲时的实际滑点。

尤其要区分两类情况：

一种是策略本身没有意识到风险，订单始终留在市场上，直到被 Toxic Flow 击中。

另一种是策略已经意识到风险，也发送了 Cancel Request，但在撤单真正生效之前，订单还是被成交了。

前者更偏向预测与决策问题，后者则是执行与系统问题。两者在最终 PnL 上可能长得差不多，但优化方法完全不同。

尾部专项优化最有意思的一点是：它不一定需要提高策略的预测能力。

有时候，你完全不需要预测未来价格，只需要识别哪些市场状态下，自己的订单风险会突然变得不对称，然后选择不参与。

当然，这里还要算一笔账。

如果为了避免最差的 1% 成交，你同时放弃了巨量正常盈利机会，那么这套优化未必值得；更严格的做法是对比优化前后的完整 PnL 分布，并通过订单回放估计被撤掉的订单原本是否会成交。

最终衡量的应该是净收益与尾部损失是否改善，而不是单纯把 Markout 胜率刷得更漂亮。

实际上，对于一套已经能够稳定赚取微小价差的高频策略来说，继续把正常行情下的平均收益提高 0.5bps，可能需要投入大量研发精力。

但如果能识别某类极端亏损场景，并且用很低的机会成本将它过滤掉，带来的收益改善可能更明显。

前提是，这些尾部亏损具有可提前识别的结构性特征，而不是事后从噪声中挑出来的规律。

text:
👊 Warsh refused to signal a hike and the market cheered. Read what it actually priced 

🌡
"I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year." That is the whole rate content of the speech.
Hike odds for 28 October fell to about 17% from roughly 30% while he was still talking.

⚠️ But the hike did not disappear. It moved.

🔸 Before CPI on Tuesday: 22% for October

🔸 After CPI: somewhere between 42% and 54%, depending which tracker you read

🔸 During Warsh's remarks: back to ~17%

🔸 December: 77% to 89%, and traders are now pricing the chance of two hikes or a half-point move in one go
* In plain English: the market did not decide the Fed is done. It decided the Fed waits, and then does more at once. That is a deferral, not a reprieve.

🧚‍♂️ The more interesting part was not about rates at all. Warsh spent most of the session on AI — a major benefit to the US economy, something that will change how monetary policy is conducted, and the end of worrying about secular stagnation. He also said he has no idea what it does to jobs over the next 12 to 18 months, and that the path will be "very bumpy."

💭 So the Fed chair is underwriting an AI productivity boom in the same week the market repriced AI debt: CoreWeave's 2032 bonds at 15%, TSMC posting a record quarter and falling 11.5% anyway, chipmakers leading two days of selling in Asia.
One of those two readings is wrong. The December meeting is where it gets settled.

🔸 BTC reclaimed the 50-day near $81k. $87k is still the level that has rejected it three times this month

text:
Banger paper from Google DeepMind on long-horizon multi-agent coding.

(bookmark it)

They report that, to the best of their knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents.

They report that four Gemini 4 Argon agents beat Minecraft end-to-end. They defeated the Ender Dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes with no human intervention.

Each agent controlled one player through the standard Mineflayer library. No one assigned roles, wrote game logic, or scouted a seed in advance. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves, and coordinated through in-game chat and a shared memory.

Over the run, they wrote 2,783 programs and died 605 times. They split the work, shared what they learned, and recovered each other's items after deaths.

If you build agents for long software or enterprise tasks, this is a useful case study. The team had to keep one plan consistent across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day.

https://t.co/h1Z87NYKqp

今天发布今年第 19 款产品 sofatap（沙发瘫），开始 TestFlight 公测！

这两周我大部分 vibe coding 其实不是在书房做的，而是在客厅，用接着电视的那台电脑。agent 在跑任务，我窝在沙发和啵啵一起看电视剧或者是打游戏，需要点一下、回一句的时候，要起身去找键盘鼠标，很不方便…

所以我给自己做了 sofatap：把 iPhone 变成触控板和键盘，躺在沙发上就能操作电视上的电脑，Mac、Windows、Linux 都能用，最新版本还支持索尼和小米的 Google TV。

我一直觉得，现在的个人电脑其实无处不在，但我们不该再被绑在它面前，用坐在桌前、手按键鼠的老方式去用它。sofatap 是第一步。接下来我想让它支持语音，直接跟 agent 说一声，让它全自动去操作电脑。

开源，免费，也在客厅写代码的朋友来试试，有问题直接回复我：

我反复强调了两年，最核心的问题就是散热问题，这是物理定律，根本无解。

quotedTweet.text:
今年YC投的一个最傻逼的项目：把data center发射到太空。

他们的想法是，既然SpaceX发射成本低，太空中太阳能用不完，散热成本低，还有Starlink等几家通信供应商，

索性把data center发射到太空中，比在地球上供电要便宜。

下面我来简单证明一下这个项目为什么是大傻逼：

他们给出的理由在图2，如果一个data center运行10年，最大的成本在于电价，10年需要花费1亿刀电费；

但实际情况是，你在地球上任何一个地方，投资200万刀的钱（无论是撒哈拉沙漠，还是某个新加坡填海出来的小岛），铺设一大坨同等投入成本的光伏太阳能设备，成本完全相同，而且同样完全够给冷却系统供电。

这个项目的核心价值在于，用现实中的10年电费，去对比一次性投入10年寿命的光伏太阳能系统，但问题是，这个东西现实中也可以部署在地表，并且你的冷却系统也不一定能保证更高效（在地面甚至可以用海水）。

我个人建议，这个项目不如调整方向，在夏威夷附近填海造几个岛，做好防水，然后从中国拉几十集装箱的光伏太阳能板，做好水冷——比把整个data center发射上天划算100倍。

他们的想法是，既然SpaceX发射成本低，太空中太阳能用不完，散热成本低，还有Starlink等几家通信供应商，

索性把data center发射到太空中，比在地球上供电要便宜。

下面我来简单证明一下这个项目为什么是大傻逼： https://t.co/2PJlxOqg7p

result.text:
今年YC投的一个最傻逼的项目：把data center发射到太空。

他们的想法是，既然SpaceX发射成本低，太空中太阳能用不完，散热成本低，还有Starlink等几家通信供应商，

索性把data center发射到太空中，比在地球上供电要便宜。

下面我来简单证明一下这个项目为什么是大傻逼：

他们给出的理由在图2，如果一个data center运行10年，最大的成本在于电价，10年需要花费1亿刀电费；

但实际情况是，你在地球上任何一个地方，投资200万刀的钱（无论是撒哈拉沙漠，还是某个新加坡填海出来的小岛），铺设一大坨同等投入成本的光伏太阳能设备，成本完全相同，而且同样完全够给冷却系统供电。

这个项目的核心价值在于，用现实中的10年电费，去对比一次性投入10年寿命的光伏太阳能系统，但问题是，这个东西现实中也可以部署在地表，并且你的冷却系统也不一定能保证更高效（在地面甚至可以用海水）。

我个人建议，这个项目不如调整方向，在夏威夷附近填海造几个岛，做好防水，然后从中国拉几十集装箱的光伏太阳能板，做好水冷——比把整个data center发射上天划算100倍。

text:
🧵 Estas son las cuentas que más leo sobre AI.

1. @bcherny: lidera Claude Code en Anthropic. Cuenta en primera persona cómo programa con Claude: prompts reales, verificación formal con Lean/TLA+ y cómo trabaja el equipo por dentro.

2. @hwchase17: CEO de LangChain. Piensa en voz alta sobre harnesses, memoria, subagentes async, evals y routing de modelos, con números de sus propios agentes en producción.

3. @LangChain: novedades de LangSmith y Deep Agents, y casos de empresas que ya corren agentes en producción (evals, trazas, contexto largo).

4. @rauchg: CEO de Vercel. Datos de cómo los agentes ya están desplegando y comprando infraestructura, y opiniones sobre CLIs, Rust y cómo diseñar software para agentes.

5. @amasad: CEO de Replit. Visión de producto sobre agentes que construyen apps y negocios, seguridad en apps de escritorio con IA y el impacto de la IA en la economía.

6. @santtiagom_: en español, desde MercadoLibre. Explica conceptos de agentes (durabilidad, prompt injection, permisos) y comparte guías y papers que vale la pena guardar.

7. @MatthewBerman: prueba los modelos nuevos el día que salen y muestra qué tal funcionan en tareas reales. Útil para hacerse una idea rápida antes de probarlos uno mismo.

8. @0xMovez: hilos y artículos largos sobre setups con Claude: skills, MCPs, reverse engineering, motion design. Tono muy entusiasta, pero los recursos que comparte son concretos.

9. @kirillk_web3: noticias diarias de IA y repos open source que se están moviendo en GitHub. Bueno para no perderse lo que está pasando.

10. @ParamSiddh: ingeniero de IA con opiniones cortas sobre vibe coding y qué modelo usar para cada cosa (planear, ejecutar, revisar).

对动画的理解，还得是日本人。

一位日本开发者把动画设计中常用的专业术语，整理成了一个可以直接喂给 AI 的资源库。

涵盖镜头语言、UI 组件、动态图形等 5 大领域，足足 120 个动态效果案例，而且每个都有直观的动画演示。

使用方法也特别简单：

直接把这个 GitHub 项目扔给 Claude Code 或 Codex，让 AI 浏览动效库，挑选你喜欢的效果，再告诉它用在哪里。

以前需要绞尽脑汁描述半天的动画，现在只需要给 AI 一个参考，它就知道你想要什么。

那些默默努力，把人类已有的知识整理好、再交给 AI 的人，值得我们永远尊敬。

text:
This really should not be difficult. A postseason system should aim to accomplish two things: 

1) Every member/participant in the sport should have a clear and controllable path to the ultimate championship. This addresses the basic standards of fairness. 

2) Once condition 1 is met, the aim of the postseason system should then be to get as many of the best teams into the system as possible. 

Applying these principles to the FBS level of D1 college football, the teams in a 24-team playoff should be selected as follows: 

1) Every FBS conference champion gets an automatic bid. It is up to the conferences to determine their champion - season record, championship games, whatever. This fills 10 of the 24 slots. 

2) The remaining 14 slots go to the 14 best remaining teams. I don't really care how this is determined - committee, AP Poll, Coaches, computers, whatever. 

This simple selection system ensures that every one of the 138 teams in the FBS knows from day one of the season what they can do to guarantee themselves a spot in the playoffs and to win the natty. 

All of the arguments between the 6th best SEC team and the 4th best Big 12 team or whatever are fun but ultimately immaterial. No team can really claim they were hard done for, because every team controlled its own destiny from week one. 

If you feel so strongly that the MAC or Sun Belt or whatever conference does not deserve an automatic bid, the solution is to relegate that conference to the FCS - not to abandon the first principle.

text:
Reflection AI 最有意思的地方，是它一边借鉴 DeepSeek-V3 的 MoE 路由设计，一边跑到华盛顿，把中国开源模型的领先定义为美国的国家安全威胁。

今天 Reflection 正式开放了 Beam 1.0 的模型权重，5010 亿总参数、230 亿激活参数，Apache 2.0 协议，支持 100 万 Token 上下文。

模型本身其实没有那么惊艳。按照 Reflection 自己公布的成绩，DeepSWE v1.1 上 Beam 得分 44.4，Kimi K3 是 68.0。其他多项 Agent 测试里，中国模型也依然领先。Beam 更值得讨论的卖点是推理效率。

但发布当天，AWS、Google Cloud、微软 Azure、NVIDIA、Cloudflare、CoreWeave、Dell、HPE 等 40 多家合作伙伴已经就位，从云端推理到企业私有部署，几乎全部覆盖。

今年 5 月，Reflection CEO Misha Laskin 在华盛顿游说时就公开讲过，中国正在大幅领先开源 AI，而这构成了美国的国家安全威胁。Reflection 当时已经拿到了 250 亿美元的估值。

他的逻辑其实很清楚。当一个国家的政府或一家大型企业决定把 AI 部署进自己的基础设施里，模型的国籍、监管归属、供应链控制权都会进入采购决策。

所以 Reflection 的商业机会非常微妙。它可以在性能尚未达到中国头部模型水平的时候，先争取那些愿意为了供应链安全和政治确定性付费的客户。技术上的差距可以慢慢追，企业采购中的信任壁垒却可能提前建立。

中国开源模型接下来真正需要面对的，是一个相当残酷的商业问题。

我们把模型性能做到了世界前列，把推理成本压了下来，也让全球开发者从中国的技术创新中获益。可这些技术一旦成为全行业共享的基础，美国公司完全可以在此之上继续开发，再利用本土身份、资本和政府关系，去争取利润更高的企业合同。

最讽刺的是，这整个过程完全符合开源精神。

开源可以让技术成果跨越国界，却无法保证创造这些成果的公司最终获得相应的商业回报。

中国模型已经证明自己有能力影响全球 AI 的技术路线。至于能从中赚到多少钱，我觉得现在还远远没到可以庆祝的时候。
